item.title: Higher Tripos Theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.27163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tripos theory constructs categorical models of higher-order logic from indexed logical data. We develop higher tripos theory and higher tripos-to-topos construction recovering the classical construction on zero-types through a covering criterion. The higher tripos-to-topos construction yields elementary $\infty$-toposes with closed bounded hierarchies of univalent universes, thus establishing a logical adjunction between $\infty$-triposes and elementary $\infty$-toposes with univalent universes. We also construct a logically conservative higher completion of regular $1$-categories with weak section families and a finite-limit-closed projective cover. This completion preserves original maps, predicates, and existing dependent products, and gives criteria for extending interpretations while preserving logical structure. With strongly inaccessible size bounds, Kleene assemblies instantiate the construction, producing a cumulative hierarchy of univalent universes that classifies every family in the completion and recovering the effective topos as the category of zero-types. We then establish an arithmetical completeness result: for a uniformly computably presented family, the numerical index set for identity with a fixed classifier code is $\Pi^0_2$-complete. We also construct two inequivalent univalent classifiers with the same global homotopy type: every internal map from one to the natural-number object is constant, whereas the other admits a nonconstant such map. These reconstruction, preservation, and computability results contribute to the higher effective-topos program of Awodey-Emmenegger and Anel-Awodey-Barton.
item.dc:creator: Yoshihiro Maruyama

item.title: Natural Deduction Derivations as Directed Acyclic Proof Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.27196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In conventional natural deduction, a proof of a proposition is a derivation tree constructed out of inference rules with some number of premises and a conclusion judgement. For propositional logic, in contrast to the other connectives, the rule for disjunction elimination of $A \vee B$ involves concluding with an auxiliary formula C from $A \vdash C$ and $B \vdash C$. Not only is this asymmetry unsightly, it also introduces the need for commuting conversions across disjunction eliminations to transform between proof derivations that are morally equivalent but not $\beta\eta$-equivalent. To resolve the asymmetry, Jean-Yves Girard suggests a disjunction elimination rule with multiple conclusions A and B, but claims that "we have no way of bringing them back together". In this work, we pursue Girard's proposal using the key insight that proof derivations need not be trees, but may be directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in general. Derivation rules are represented as nodes, premises as incoming edges, and conclusions as outgoing edges. Treating derivations as DAGs permits using the alternate rule by ensuring that the subderivations pointed at by each conclusion eventually join up at a new concluding node. Commuting conversions can then be formulated in terms of interactions with this join node. We explore ways to design a proof graph language with reduction and commutation rules such that proof simplification retains its concluding judgements, i.e. type preservation. In particular, we examine two styles of reduction rules: a local style, which only requires looking at the relevant subgraph of a whole proof but necessitates a number of extraneous constructs to satisfy type preservation; and a global style, which doesn't require all the extraneous constructs but necessitates looking at the entire proof graph as a whole.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Chan, Aaron Stump

item.title: Theorem prover Arend
item.description: arXiv:2610.27264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper is an exposition of the theorem prover Arend developed at JetBrains Research. Arend language has been designed to facilitate the formalization of mathematics within the framework of univalent foundations and with the focus on constructive mathematics. It is based on a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax that is more closely aligned with Martin-L\"of Type Theory (MLTT) than fully computational cubical type theories, while still retaining some of their computational properties useful in practice. Among the most notable features of the Arend language is its powerful system of classes and records supporting subsumptive subtyping, partial implementations and anonymous extensions, which provides extensive flexibility for constructing hierarchies of definitions. Formalization in Arend is streamlined by the IntelliJ Arend plugin, which transforms IntelliJ IDEA into a full-fledged integrated development environment (IDE) for the Arend language. The main Arend library arend-lib includes formalizations in constructive algebra, topology and synthetic homotopy theory.
item.dc:creator: Fedor Part, Valery Isaev, Sergey Sinchuk

item.title: Containment of Conjunctive Queries with Negative Information over Semirings
item.description: arXiv:2610.27957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the containment problem for (unions of) conjunctive queries ((U)CQs) with negative information on semiring-annotated databases. Our approach to negative information follows the treatment of negation proposed by Gr\"adel and Tannen (2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024) for first-order logic and fixed point logic which applies productively to large classes of semirings, including bounded distributive lattices, as well as the important provenance semirings studied for positive CQ containment by Green (2009). Negation features in (U)CQs along two dimensions: negated equalities (disequations), and negated relational atoms. We study complexity for each of them separately, as well as jointly. For disequations, we extend a methodology that proves the same complexity bounds as the ones already known for the standard Boolean semiring (in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) for most semirings of interest. Two prominent exceptions are $\mathbb{N}[X]$ and Trio(X) where the complexity bound for containment is in the second level of the counting hierarchy. For CQs with negated relational atoms we show that the complexity, surprisingly, is the same as that of the containment of CQs without negation when one considers model-defining and provenance-tracking interpretations (namely, nondeterministic polynomial time). Interestingly, among bounded distributive lattices, the Boolean two-element case is the only one where the complexity of the problem continues to be hard for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy for model-defining interpretations. Furthermore, we show that the complexity increases again for distributive lattices if we focus on other classes of interpretations. Finally, we consider queries that have both negated equalities and negated relational atoms and show that the complexity of containment continues to be that of the case with just negated equalities.
item.dc:creator: Guillermo Badia, Carles Noguera, Gaia Petreni, Alice Portone, Val Tannen

item.title: A General Construction of Strict Models in HoTT
item.description: arXiv:2610.28370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Homotopy type theory (HoTT) provides a natural setting for studying the metatheory of type theory, as it comes with additional extensionality principles compared to ordinary Martin-L\"of type theory. In particular, it is especially suitable for developing semantics of type theory, where one distinguishes two kinds of models: strict models, which give us sound interpretations, and pseudomodels. Pseudomodels are useful as they occur prevalently and can be turned into strict models by constructions called strictifications. However, the commonly used strictifications do not translate well to HoTT, as they require assumptions that are generally not satisfied by concrete examples of models. We show how to carry out the universe model construction, due to Voevodsky, in HoTT. Under this construction, every pseudomodel together with a universe type closed under enough type formers gives rise to a strict model. We also show how to interpret type formers in the resulting model assuming that the universe is closed under them. Finally, we demonstrate that this construction generalises existing instances of strict set models in the literature, and we apply it to more examples, yielding presheaf models and assembly models of type theory in HoTT. Our results are formalised in Rocq using the UniMath library.
item.dc:creator: Niyousha Najmaei, Niels van der Weide

item.title: Linear Axiomatization of Linear Differential Equations
item.description: arXiv:2610.28460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article presents an axiomatization of linear differential equations that is complete for topologically open properties with compact initial conditions and time horizons by proving them deductively via a sound reduction to formulas of linear real arithmetic. Indeed, linearity is preserved: linear differential invariants are complete for open properties of linear differential equations and reduce with a linear number of Lie derivatives (per atom) to linear real arithmetic. In particular, this article shows that the linear fragment of differential dynamic logic (dL), a modal extension of standard first-order logic over the reals satisfies these completeness properties. By establishing completeness within decidable linear real arithmetic, the need for proving sophisticated nonlinear formulas of real arithmetic is circumvented. Furthermore, this article establishes generalizations to the nonlinear fragment of dL that enable the practical certification of reachability computations, validating the output of external computations in dL with machine-checkable proofs.
item.dc:creator: Long Qian, Andr\'e Platzer

item.title: Privacy-Preserving Robustness-Guided Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.27441v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In industries like semi-conductors and aerospace, it is common for the design company to contract out part of the testing process to a Testing-as-a-Service (TaaS) company. In such a setup, both parties want to keep their intellectual property private (i.e. unknown to the other party): namely the design and its output traces for the designer, and the detailed correctness specifications for the tester. We demonstrate a practical way for conducting provably private TaaS using a cryptographically secure multi-party computation protocol. We do so for the common setup where the specification is in Signal Temporal Logic, and testing is done using robustness-guided falsification. Our implementation carefully separates the steps of falsification, and manages to be $\textit{maximally secure}$, in the sense that the parties learn the absolutely minimum necessary for falsification. For up to a 100-dimensional input search space, the generation of one test takes less than 80 msec, and the overhead of the privacy-preserving protocol is less than 6x. These numbers mean that privacy-preserving TaaS is practical, thus enabling TaaS in security-sensitive industries.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: IEEE Embedded Systems Letters vol. 18 no. 5 (2026) 353-356
item.dc:creator: Charles Koll, Houssam Abbas, Mike Rosulek

item.title: Rational polynomial solvability reduces to stratifiability of semilinear sets
item.description: arXiv:2610.27482v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A semilinear set is stratifiable if it is a finite union of linear sets whose periods have at most two nonzero coordinates, with no two periods in one component connecting alternating pairs of coordinates. We give a computable many-one reduction from the existence of a rational zero of an integer polynomial to deciding stratifiability. After the classical reduction to quadratic systems, we reduce rational solvability of these systems to a problem we call finite separation by Cartesian products of rational linear forms. Its input consists of rational subspaces $D_1,\ldots,D_k\le\mathbb Q^r\times\mathbb Q^r$. A separator is a map $(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)\mapsto(u(\boldsymbol x),v(\boldsymbol y))$, where $u,v\colon\mathbb Q^r\to\mathbb Q$ are nonzero rational linear forms. The problem asks whether finitely many separators suffice so that every pair outside $\bigcup_iD_i$ receives, from some separator, a value attained at no pair in that union. We then reduce this problem to stratifiability. Ginsburg and Spanier's characterization of letter-bounded context-free languages} also induces a reduction from rational polynomial solvability to context-freeness of letter-bounded languages specified by semilinear exponent sets. An OpenAI preprint claims undecidability of rational polynomial solvability; if correct, our result settles the decidability of general stratifiability, a problem open since 1966.
item.dc:creator: Micha\"el Cadilhac

item.title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.27620v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.
item.dc:creator: Anmol Pandey, Aditya Jain, Liang Chen, Carsten Maple

item.title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
item.description: arXiv:2610.28484v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.
item.dc:creator: Carlo Ciliberto, Alessandro Rudi, Enrico Tassi

item.title: What is a Good Projection?: Correctness and Separation Results of End-Point Projections
item.description: arXiv:2610.28525v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: \emph{Multiparty session types} (MPST) is a type discipline for ensuring distributed programs are implemented correctly \emph{by construction}. MPST starts by specifying a choreographic protocol as a \emph{global type} and \emph{projects} it onto each participant, generating \emph{local types} with a guarantee of type soundness and deadlock-freedom. A central issue of MPST is that its type soundness is fragile, as it must be proven each time with respect to a chosen projection algorithm under specific semantics with a specific program correctness goal. To overcome this problem, we propose general criteria for a \emph{good projection} -- a set of requirements for projection algorithms by which type soundness, deadlock-freedom and liveness of distributed programs are \emph{automatically} derived. Using the criteria, we prove that 8 distinct projections in the literature are good under both synchronous and asynchronous semantics, and that 4 are incorrect, failing type soundness. We extend the good projection criteria to mixed choice global types and asynchronous communication optimisations, proposing new ``good projection'' algorithms. We apply properties of good projections to prove \emph{separation} and \emph{expressiveness} results over the projection algorithms and MPST typing systems. Having a generalised typing system that is robust with respect to the good projection criteria, we provide an implementation with mixed choice global types that is \emph{modular} with respect to a chosen projection algorithm and desired program properties. Our separation results help programmers make informed trade-offs between complexity and expressiveness when choosing projection algorithms, and our theory ensures their chosen algorithms are correctly applied.
item.dc:creator: Jake Masters, Nobuko Yoshida

item.title: Forall-Exists Relational Verification by Filtering to Forall-Forall
item.description: arXiv:2509.04777v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Relational verification encompasses reasoning about data abstraction, security and privacy, secure compilation, and functional specification of tensor programs, among others. Several relational logics and tools support compositional reasoning about $\forall\forall$ (2-safety) properties and, generally, $k$-safety properties. In contrast, few logics and tools exist for reasoning about $\forall\exists$ properties which are critical in the presence of nondeterminism. This paper's primary contribution is a technique for verifying a $\forall\exists$ judgment by way of a novel transformation. The filter-adequacy transformation adds assertions to a product program in such a way that the desired $\forall\exists$ property (of a pair of underlying unary programs) is implied by a $\forall\forall$ property of the transformed product. The paper develops bicoms, a form of product programs that facilitates expressing good alignments and caters for direct translation of $\forall\forall$ properties to unary correctness; proves that successful $\forall\forall$ verification of a transformed bicom implies the $\forall\exists$ spec for its underlying unary commands; and evaluates the technique using a prototype auto-active relational verifier. The technique enables users to work with ordinary assertions and assumptions, and a standard assertion language, so that existing $\forall\forall$ and unary verification tools can be used for $\forall\exists$.
item.dc:creator: Ramana Nagasamudram, Anindya Banerjee, Jude Kanjamala, David A. Naumann

item.title: Just Previsions
item.description: arXiv:2605.10173v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Previsions are positively homogeneous functionals, and are generalized forms of integration functionals. We investigate previsions -- just previsions, not sublinear or superlinear previsions as in previous work. We show that every prevision can be expressed as an infimum of sublinear previsions, and as a supremum of superlinear previsions under mild conditions. This extends to homeomorphisms between spaces of previsions and certain hyperspaces over spaces of sublinear or superlinear previsions, which can also be characterized in terms of orthogonality relations, making the construction a variant of a double powerspace construction.
item.dc:creator: Jean Goubault-Larrecq

item.title: BARReL: a modern backend for Atelier B in Lean
item.description: arXiv:2606.20121v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: BARReL is a Lean 4 library bridging Atelier B, an industrial tool for the B method, and the Lean proof assistant by enabling users to conduct their formal B developments---up to machine refinement and implementation---interactively inside Lean, while retaining standard B syntax. B partial operators are encoded with explicit well-definedness conditions, using Lean's dependent types to enforce a well-definedness discipline by construction. That is, proof obligations and proof steps cannot silently rely on ill-typed or ill-defined instantiations. BARReL also provides basic automation for discharging these conditions. The implementation is written entirely using Lean metaprogramming and is designed to be modular: extending the supported B fragment typically requires only adding new syntax and encoding clauses. We compare the resulting workflow with Atelier B on a B refinement development and examine the checks required during interactive proof through two examples.
item.dc:creator: Ghilain Bergeron, Vincent Tr\'elat

item.title: Verified Purely Functional Catenable Real-Time Deques
item.description: arXiv:2505.07681v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present OCaml and Rocq implementations of Kaplan and Tarjan's purely functional, real-time catenable deques. The correctness of our Rocq code is machine-checked.
item.dc:creator: Jules Viennot, Arthur Wendling, Arma\"el Gu\'eneau, Fran\c{c}ois Pottier

item.title: Computable Quantification in Reflective Grounded Arithmetic
item.description: arXiv:2607.25533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Informal statements of G\"odel's incompleteness theorems often run: "any consistent formal system with arithmetic has true but unprovable statements." That reading assumes a classical notion of truth, under which a universal statement is true as soon as each of its numeral instances is. This paper presents reflective grounded arithmetic (RGA), in which truth is grounded in computation and universal quantification is grounded reflectively: a universal statement is true when the system's own proof search certifies its schematic instance, and false when the system refutes one numeral instance. RGA allows recursive definitions without restriction and proves addition, multiplication and Ackermann's function total as theorems quantified inside the system. RGA is consistent, and it is complete for its own, grounded notion of truth: every well-formed statement that evaluates to true is provable. G\"odel's theorems still hold for RGA, as a companion paper shows. The statements that classical reasoning calls true but unprovable have every numeral instance provable but no certified schematic instance, so they are ungrounded in RGA; read instance by instance, in an $\omega$-semantics for which RGA is also sound, they are true. All results are machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL: soundness and consistency; completeness for grounded truth, open statements included; $\omega$-soundness and $\omega$-consistency; that grounded truth is recursively enumerable and RGA represents exactly the recursively enumerable sets; and $\omega$-incompleteness. The logic is neither classical nor intuitionistic: double negation is eliminable as an entailment, excluded middle fails wherever a statement has no boolean value, RGA has the disjunction and witness properties, and the deduction theorem holds exactly at provably decided hypotheses.
item.dc:creator: Bryan Ford

item.title: Noise-aware Verification and Synthesis of Quantum Programs
item.description: arXiv:2608.05807v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work provides a comprehensive framework for noise-aware quantum program analysis, ranging from logical foundations to model checking and automated synthesis. While most research on quantum programming considers an idealized, noise-free semantics for quantum programs, we reason about quantum programs that are executed on real, noisy hardware. We use the error models published by quantum-hardware vendors to give a hardware-dependent semantics to quantum programs. We then present a noise-aware quantum Hoare logic with a relatively complete proof system. We finally use state-space exploration techniques for the hardware-aware verification and synthesis of loop-free quantum programs. In this way, we synthesize optimal, hardware-dependent solutions for parity bit-flip, GHZ state preparation, and other problems that commonly occur as subroutines in larger quantum algorithms. We evaluate our method on all 55 hardware specifications provided by the IBM Qiskit toolkit. Finally, we also show that classical probabilistic branching is needed for optimality in quantum programming.
item.dc:creator: Stefanie Muroya, Krishnendu Chatterjee, Thomas A. Henzinger
